title: Design by nature: The influence of windows on cognitive performance and affect
authors: L.A. Sharam, K.M. Mayer, O. Baumann
research_question: To examine the impact of window views of nature on affect and cognitive functioning.

participants.description: Experiment 1: 55 adults (37 females, 18 males; Mage = 24 years, SD = 9). Experiment 2: 57 adults (40 females, 17 males; Mage = 24.89, SD = 7.18). All participants had normal or corrected vision and hearing.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Custom-made VR simulations of office rooms (~20 m²) with identical features (white walls, carpet, wooden desk, loudspeaker, door, ceiling lamp). Three conditions: 1) Nature-view (three windows with static view of treetops and blue skies), 2) No-window (three blue panels of same size as windows, blocking view), 3) Daylight (windows with shutters allowing daylight infiltration but blocking view of nature, used only in Experiment 2).

mechanisms: Enhanced positive affect may have influenced the ability to engage in divergent thinking.
Increased motivation, which in turn is mediated by more positive affectivity.
Natural elements within the environment invoke a reduction in the stress response, resulting in the restoration of mood states.
moderators: Cognitive fatigue (discussed as a potential factor for null effects on alertness/attention)
implementation_implications: Architects, interior designers, and developers should endeavour to incorporate window views of foliage and additional biophilic features within interior designs to enhance affect, cognitive performance, and wellbeing.
Nature-based VR could be used and further evaluated within various fields such as clinical psychology, health, education, as a tool for improving wellbeing.

tables.description: Descriptive statistics for all continuous variables (N = 57) across No-window, Daylight, and Nature-view conditions for positive affect (PA), negative affect (NA), simple reaction time task (SRTT), 2-back discrimination score (DS), and 2-back reaction time (RT).

limitations: The obviousness of the experimental manipulation and within-subjects design could create a potential for expectation and social desirability bias.
The use of blue shutters and panels might have minimized the visual contrast to the biophilic condition or been perceived as a 'blocked-window' rather than a 'no-window' condition.

The study examined window views within office-like settings; future research should utilize more diverse population groups in differing environmental settings (e.g., hospitals, classrooms, or residential settings).

The use of self-reported measures of affect may create limitations to the internal validity of the study due to social desirability bias; future research could consider utilizing objective physiological measures.
VR simulations are artificially created and do not include additional sensory information (e.g., temperature).

Participants in the current study were not cognitively fatigued, which may have diminished any potential effect of nature exposure on lower-level (alertness) or higher-level (executive attention) functions.

The exposure duration (approximately 10-min per environmental condition) might have been insufficient for full cognitive restoration, as ART suggests longer durations are needed for different levels of restoration.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments, even virtual ones, can restore directed attention and improve cognitive performance and positive affect.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper investigates how exposure to natural window views in a virtual office environment leads to improved cognitive performance and affect by facilitating attention restoration processes, characterized by soft fascination and reduced mental effort.

steps.to_construct: Increased positive affect / Reduced negative affect
